summary: APT29, widely known as Cozy Bear, is a Russian state-sponsored cyberespionage group assessed to operate on behalf of Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), active since at least 2008 and linked to the 2016 DNC breach and the 2020 SolarWinds/Sunburst supply-chain attack.

title: Core Security Technologies
summary: Core Security Technologies is an information-security company founded in 1996 in Buenos Aires, Argentina, best known for creating the commercial penetration-testing platform Core Impact and for its long association with the open-source network-protocol toolkit Impacket.

title: CrowdStrike
summary: CrowdStrike is an American cybersecurity company founded in 2011 by George Kurtz, Dmitri Alperovitch, and Gregg Marston, known for its cloud-native Falcon endpoint protection platform and for its 2016 investigation attributing the Democratic National Committee hack to Russian state-linked groups.

title: Equation Group
summary: The Equation Group is a highly sophisticated cyberespionage actor publicly identified and named by Kaspersky Lab researchers in February 2015, whose tools, techniques, and operational details have led researchers and journalists to widely link it to the U.S. National Security Agency; a subset of its hacking tools was later stolen and leaked by a group calling itself the Shadow Brokers.

title: Hacking Team
summary: Hacking Team was a Milan-based company that sold offensive intrusion and surveillance software to governments and police forces worldwide, until a July 2015 breach by the hacker Phineas Fisher exposed roughly 400 gigabytes of its internal emails, source code, and client list.

title: Lazarus Group
summary: Lazarus Group is a state-sponsored cyber threat actor widely attributed to North Korea, active since at least 2009 and linked to the 2014 Sony Pictures hack, the 2016 Bangladesh Bank SWIFT heist, and the 2017 WannaCry ransomware outbreak.

title: Mandiant
summary: Mandiant is a cybersecurity firm specializing in incident response and threat intelligence, founded in 2004 by Kevin Mandia, best known for its 2013 "APT1" report publicly attributing years of cyber espionage against U.S. and other organizations to a Chinese military unit.

title: NSO Group
summary: NSO Group is an Israeli technology company, founded in 2010, best known for developing Pegasus, a commercial "zero-click" spyware suite sold to government clients and later linked to widespread surveillance of journalists, activists, lawyers, and political figures worldwide.

title: Zero Day Initiative (ZDI)
summary: The Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) is a vendor-agnostic vulnerability purchase and coordinated-disclosure program started on July 25, 2005 by TippingPoint, a division of 3Com, and led today by Trend Micro following its 2015 acquisition of HP TippingPoint.

title: Computer Underground Digest
summary: Computer Underground Digest (CuD) was a weekly electronic newsletter published from March 1990 to March 2000 that covered the legal, social, and cultural issues surrounding the early computer underground, edited by Jim Thomas with Gordon Meyer as news editor.

title: Countdown to Zero Day: Stuxnet and the Launch of the World's First Digital Weapon
summary: "Countdown to Zero Day" is a 2014 nonfiction book by American investigative journalist Kim Zetter, published by Crown, that chronicles the discovery and technical analysis of the Stuxnet computer worm and its sabotage of Iran's Natanz uranium-enrichment facility.

title: Ghost in the Wires: My Adventures as the World's Most Wanted Hacker
summary: "Ghost in the Wires" is a 2011 memoir by Kevin Mitnick, co-written with William L. Simon, recounting Mitnick's years as a computer intruder and phone phreaker, his time as a federal fugitive, and his 1995 arrest.

title: Kingpin: How One Hacker Took Over the Billion-Dollar Cybercrime Underground
summary: "Kingpin" is a 2011 non-fiction book by journalist and former hacker Kevin Poulsen, published by Crown, that chronicles the rise and fall of Max Ray Butler (a.k.a. "Max Vision" and "Iceman"), a hacker who stole access to roughly 1.8 million credit card accounts and took over rival carding forums to build the unified marketplace CardersMarket.

title: The RISKS Digest
summary: The RISKS Digest, formally the "Forum On Risks to the Public in Computers and Related Systems," is a moderated mailing list and Usenet newsgroup (comp.risks) documenting failures, vulnerabilities, and unintended consequences of computer systems, moderated by Peter G. Neumann since its founding on August 1, 1985.

title: Sandworm: A New Era of Cyberwar and the Hunt for the Kremlin's Most Dangerous Hackers
summary: "Sandworm" is a 2019 nonfiction book by American journalist Andy Greenberg, published by Doubleday, that chronicles the investigation into a Russian military-intelligence hacking group and its escalating cyberattacks, culminating in the 2017 NotPetya malware outbreak.

title: The Art of Deception
summary: "The Art of Deception: Controlling the Human Element of Security" is a 2002 book by former hacker Kevin D. Mitnick and co-author William L. Simon, published by John Wiley & Sons, that explains how social engineering is used to bypass technical security controls.

title: Binary Ninja
summary: Binary Ninja is a commercial interactive disassembler, decompiler, and binary analysis platform developed by Vector 35, first released publicly in July 2016 as an alternative to IDA Pro for reverse engineers.

title: Cain & Abel
summary: Cain & Abel was a free Windows password recovery and network analysis tool created by Italian developer Massimiliano Montoro, combining packet sniffing, ARP spoofing, and password-cracking techniques into a single application widely used for both legitimate security testing and credential theft during the 2000s and early 2010s.

title: Maltego
summary: Maltego is a graphical link-analysis and open-source intelligence (OSINT) platform, originally developed by the company Paterva (now Maltego Technologies GmbH), used to map relationships between people, organizations, domains, and other entities for security research, threat intelligence, and investigations.

title: OllyDbg
summary: OllyDbg is a 32-bit x86 assembler-level debugger for Microsoft Windows, created by Oleh Yuschuk, that became one of the most widely used tools of the 2000s for binary code analysis, reverse engineering, and malware analysis when source code is unavailable.

title: Responder
summary: Responder is an open-source LLMNR, NBT-NS, and mDNS poisoning tool created by Laurent Gaffié that stands up rogue authentication servers to capture NetNTLM hashes and cleartext credentials on local networks.

title: Sysinternals Suite
summary: Sysinternals is a suite of advanced Windows system-internals, diagnostic, and troubleshooting utilities — including Process Explorer, Autoruns, and Process Monitor — originally created by Mark Russinovich and Bryce Cogswell and acquired by Microsoft in 2006.

title: BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708)
summary: BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) is a critical, wormable remote code execution vulnerability in Microsoft's Remote Desktop Services affecting older Windows versions, disclosed and patched by Microsoft in May 2019.

title: Citrix Bleed (CVE-2023-4966)
summary: Citrix Bleed (CVE-2023-4966) is a critical information-disclosure vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances that let remote attackers steal valid session tokens from device memory and hijack authenticated sessions, bypassing passwords and multi-factor authentication.

title: Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195)
summary: Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195) is a race-condition flaw in the Linux kernel's copy-on-write memory handling that let unprivileged local users gain write access to read-only memory mappings and escalate to root, publicly disclosed in October 2016 after evidence of active exploitation.

title: Follina (CVE-2022-30190)
summary: Follina (CVE-2022-30190) is a remote code execution vulnerability in the Microsoft Windows Support Diagnostic Tool (MSDT), triggered via the ms-msdt URL protocol handler from malicious Microsoft Office documents, publicly disclosed in May 2022.

title: ProxyLogon (CVE-2021-26855 and related)
summary: ProxyLogon is the name given to a chain of Microsoft Exchange Server vulnerabilities, led by the pre-authentication server-side request forgery flaw CVE-2021-26855, discovered by Orange Tsai of DEVCORE and exploited at mass scale by the Chinese state-sponsored group HAFNIUM in early 2021.

title: Rowhammer
summary: Rowhammer is a hardware vulnerability class in dense DRAM chips in which repeatedly and rapidly accessing ("hammering") a memory row can cause electrical interference that flips bits in adjacent rows, potentially altering data an attacker does not have permission to touch.

title: Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472)
summary: Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472) is a critical cryptographic flaw in the Netlogon Remote Protocol used by Windows domain controllers, disclosed by Tom Tervoort of Secura in 2020, that let an unauthenticated attacker on the network take full control of an Active Directory domain.

title: POODLE (CVE-2014-3566)
summary: POODLE is a 2014 design vulnerability in SSL 3.0 that can allow a network attacker to recover plaintext from a connection forced to use the obsolete protocol.

title: FREAK (CVE-2015-0204)
summary: FREAK is a TLS weakness that could allow a network attacker to downgrade some connections to export-grade RSA encryption and factor the resulting weak key.

title: Badlock (CVE-2016-2118)
summary: Badlock is the public name for CVE-2016-2118, a Samba and Windows remote-protocol vulnerability disclosed in April 2016.

title: BlueBorne
summary: BlueBorne is a set of Bluetooth vulnerabilities disclosed by Armis in 2017 that affected implementations across Android, Windows, Linux, and older Apple platforms.

title: GHOST (CVE-2015-0235)
summary: GHOST is CVE-2015-0235, a heap-based buffer overflow in glibc name-resolution functions that affected older versions of the GNU C Library.

title: DROWN (CVE-2016-0800)
summary: DROWN is a 2016 cross-protocol attack that can use SSLv2 support to decrypt some TLS connections protected with the same RSA key.

title: EFAIL
summary: EFAIL is a class of attacks disclosed in 2018 that used weaknesses in some OpenPGP and S/MIME email-client handling to exfiltrate decrypted message content.

title: Spring4Shell (CVE-2022-22965)
summary: Spring4Shell is CVE-2022-22965, a Spring Framework data-binding vulnerability that could enable remote code execution in certain JDK 9+ and Tomcat WAR deployments.

title: THC-Hydra
summary: Fast network login/password-cracking tool maintained by The Hackers Choice.

title: VeraCrypt
summary: Open-source disk-encryption software based on TrueCrypt.

title: TrueCrypt
summary: Influential disk-encryption software whose development ended abruptly in May 2014.

title: WPScan
summary: WordPress vulnerability scanner and vulnerability-database service.

title: bettercap
summary: Open-source network reconnaissance and man-in-the-middle testing framework.

title: Gophish
summary: Open-source framework for authorized phishing-simulation campaigns.

title: Social-Engineer Toolkit (SET)
summary: Open-source social-engineering assessment framework maintained by TrustedSec.

title: drozer
summary: Open-source Android security assessment framework.

title: Alexandre Cazes
summary: Alexandre Cazes was a Canadian citizen who, under the online alias "Alpha02," created and administered AlphaBay, which grew into the largest dark web marketplace for drugs, stolen data, and other illegal goods before its 2017 takedown. He was arrested in Bangkok, Thailand in July 2017 and died in Thai police custody days later, in what Thai authorities described as an apparent suicide.

title: Amit Klein
summary: Amit Klein is an Israeli security researcher who published the 2004 whitepaper that defined HTTP response splitting and co-authored the 2005 paper that introduced HTTP request smuggling. He later held research leadership roles at Sanctum, Cyota, Trusteer and SafeBreach, and is an associate professor of computer science at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.

title: M. Angela Sasse
summary: Martina Angela Sasse is a German psychologist and computer scientist whose research established usable security as a distinct field, most influentially through the 1999 paper "Users Are Not The Enemy", co-authored with Anne Adams. She is Horst Görtz Endowed Professor of Human-Centred Security at Ruhr University Bochum and a part-time Professor of Human-Centred Technology at University College London.

title: Bill Landreth
summary: Bill Landreth, known by the handle "The Cracker", was an American teenage hacker who led the early-1980s group The Inner Circle and was prosecuted by U.S. federal authorities after intrusions into GTE's Telemail electronic mail service. He later co-wrote Out of the Inner Circle: A Hacker's Guide to Computer Security (1985) with Howard Rheingold, one of the first insider accounts of hacking published by a mainstream press.

title: Andrew "bunnie" Huang
summary: Andrew "bunnie" Huang is an American hardware engineer and hacker best known for reverse-engineering the original Xbox's security while a graduate student at MIT, publishing his findings in the book "Hacking the Xbox: An Introduction to Reverse Engineering," and for subsequent work co-founding the Chumby internet appliance and building open-source hardware projects such as NeTV and the Novena laptop.

title: Chenxi Wang
summary: Chenxi Wang is a computer scientist, security industry analyst and executive who founded Rain Capital, an early-stage venture fund focused on cybersecurity. Her doctoral research at the University of Virginia produced an early description of control-flow flattening, an obfuscation technique later nicknamed "chenxification".

title: Chris Goggans
summary: Chris Goggans, known by the handle Erik Bloodaxe, was a member of the Legion of Doom hacker group in the late 1980s and early 1990s and edited Phrack magazine from 1993 to 1995. He co-founded Comsec Data Security, an early attempt to turn underground hacking expertise into a commercial security consultancy.

title: Cindy Cohn
summary: Cindy Cohn is an American civil liberties attorney specializing in Internet law who argued Bernstein v. United States, the case in which the Ninth Circuit held that encryption source code is speech protected by the First Amendment. She spent fifteen years as legal director and general counsel of the Electronic Frontier Foundation before serving as its executive director from 2015 to 2026.

title: Collin Mulliner
summary: Collin Mulliner is a German security researcher known for pioneering work on the security of mobile telephony interfaces, including SMS and MMS fuzzing, NFC-enabled phone attacks, and Android instrumentation and patching. His research demonstrated that the messaging and baseband layers of ordinary phones were a largely unexamined and remotely reachable attack surface.

title: Nicholas Allegra
summary: Nicholas Allegra, better known by the online handle "comex," is an American security researcher who created the JailbreakMe 2.0 and 3.0 browser-based iOS jailbreak tools, which let users jailbreak an iPhone or iPad simply by visiting a website.

title: David Chaum
summary: David Chaum is an American computer scientist and cryptographer who invented the concept of digital cash and founded DigiCash, while also originating the mix network design that underlies later anonymity systems such as Tor.

title: Dawn Song
summary: Dawn Song is a Chinese-American computer scientist and professor of electrical engineering and computer sciences at the University of California, Berkeley, known for research in software security, automated binary and program analysis, applied cryptography, adversarial machine learning, and blockchain privacy. She was named a MacArthur Fellow and a Guggenheim Fellow in 2010 and an ACM Fellow in 2019.

title: Christien Rioux
summary: Christien Rioux, known by the handle DilDog, is an American computer security researcher who was a member of L0pht Heavy Industries and the Cult of the Dead Cow, wrote the original code for the Back Orifice 2000 remote administration tool, and co-founded the application security company Veracode.

title: Elias Ladopoulos
summary: Elias Ladopoulos, known by the handle Acid Phreak, is a New York technologist who co-founded the hacking group Masters of Deception in the late 1980s and was one of five members federally indicted in 1992 for intrusions into telephone company systems. After serving his sentence he worked in professional information security and later founded technology companies.

title: Eva Galperin
summary: Eva Galperin is the Director of Cybersecurity at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, where she has worked since 2007 on protecting activists, journalists, and other targeted users from malware and surveillance. She is best known for her campaign to make antivirus vendors detect stalkerware and for co-founding the Coalition Against Stalkerware.

title: Evgeniy Bogachev
summary: Evgeniy Bogachev is a Russian cybercriminal identified by U.S. authorities as the creator and operator of the GameOver Zeus botnet and the figure behind the distribution of CryptoLocker ransomware, and he remains a fugitive on the FBI's Cyber Most Wanted list with a $3 million reward for information leading to his capture.

title: Fred Cohen
summary: Fred Cohen is an American computer scientist who in 1983 conducted the first documented controlled experiments with self-replicating programs on a multi-user Unix system and who gave the computer virus its formal definition in his 1984 paper, popularising a term suggested to him by Leonard Adleman. His work established that no algorithm can perfectly detect all possible viruses.

title: Giorgio Maone
summary: Giorgio Maone is the software developer who created and maintains NoScript, a browser extension first released in 2005 that blocks JavaScript and other active web content by default and permits it only on user-trusted sites. He has been a member of the Mozilla Security Group since 2007 and works on the Tor Browser as part of the Tor Project's Applications Development Team.

title: Joe Engressia
summary: Josef Carl Engressia Jr. (1949-2007), later legally named Joybubbles, was a blind American phone phreak with absolute pitch who discovered as a child that he could whistle the 2600 Hz tone used to signal idle long-distance trunks on the Bell System network. He became one of the best-known figures of the 1960s and 1970s phone phreak subculture and was profiled in Ron Rosenbaum's 1971 Esquire article "Secrets of the Little Blue Box".

title: John Hultquist
summary: John Hultquist is an American threat intelligence analyst who worked at iSight Partners, FireEye, and Mandiant before becoming Chief Analyst at Google's Threat Intelligence Group, best known for his team's role in identifying and naming the Sandworm hacking group.

title: Jon Lech Johansen
summary: Jon Lech Johansen, widely known by the nickname "DVD Jon", is a Norwegian software engineer who as a teenager in 1999 helped release DeCSS, one of the first freely available programs able to decrypt the Content Scramble System used on commercial DVD-Video discs. He was prosecuted in Norway over the release and acquitted in 2003, and later wrote several tools that circumvented Apple's FairPlay digital rights management.

title: Kate Temkin
summary: Kate Temkin is a hardware and firmware engineer known for discovering and disclosing Fusée Gelée, an unpatchable bootROM vulnerability in NVIDIA Tegra processors (CVE-2018-6242), and for open-source USB and hardware-hacking tools including Facedancer, GreatFET, GlitchKit, and LUNA.

title: Lewis De Payne
summary: Lewis De Payne, known by the handle Rosco, is an American former phone phreaker and computer hacker who was a leading figure in the Southern California phreaking scene of the late 1970s and 1980s and an early close associate of Kevin Mitnick. He was charged as Mitnick's co-defendant in the 25-count federal indictment returned in Los Angeles in September 1996.

title: Fabian Faessler
summary: Fabian Faessler, known online as LiveOverflow, is a German security researcher and educator whose YouTube channel, started in March 2015, teaches capture-the-flag technique, binary and browser exploitation, fuzzing and game hacking. He is also the founder and CEO of the Berlin company Security Flag GmbH, registered in January 2019.

title: Lorrie Faith Cranor
summary: Lorrie Faith Cranor is an American computer scientist and engineering-and-public-policy researcher at Carnegie Mellon University, where she directs the CyLab Security and Privacy Institute and the CyLab Usable Privacy and Security Laboratory (CUPS). She helped establish usable privacy and security as a research field, chaired the W3C Platform for Privacy Preferences (P3P) working group, founded the Symposium on Usable Privacy and Security (SOUPS), and served as Chief Technologist of the U.S. Federal Trade Commission in 2016.

title: Loyd Blankenship
summary: Loyd Blankenship, known by the handle The Mentor, is an American hacker and game designer who wrote The Conscience of a Hacker, the 1986 Phrack essay universally known as The Hacker Manifesto. His employment at Steve Jackson Games placed him at the centre of the 1990 US Secret Service raid that produced the landmark case Steve Jackson Games, Inc. v. United States Secret Service.

title: Maksim Yakubets
summary: Maksim Viktorovich Yakubets is a Russian national identified by US and UK authorities as the leader of Evil Corp, the Moscow-based group behind the Dridex banking malware. He was indicted in the United States and sanctioned by the US Treasury on 5 December 2019, when the State Department also announced a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest.

title: Marcia Hofmann
summary: Marcia Clare Hofmann is an American attorney known for her work on electronic privacy, computer crime law and free expression, including years as a staff attorney and special counsel at the Electronic Frontier Foundation. She has defended programmers and security researchers in high-profile computer crime cases, among them the appeals of Andrew "weev" Auernheimer and the Lavabit encryption-key dispute.

title: Mark Abene
summary: Mark Abene, known by the handle Phiber Optik, is an American hacker who belonged to both the Legion of Doom and the New York group Masters of Deception, and who became one of the best-known defendants of the early 1990s federal crackdown on computer intrusion. After serving a one-year federal sentence and being released in November 1994, he worked as an information security consultant and public speaker.

title: Mark Curphey
summary: Mark Curphey is a software and security practitioner who started the Open Web Application Security Project (OWASP) in 2001, the open community effort that became one of the most widely referenced sources of web application security guidance. He later founded the software composition analysis company SourceClear and co-founded Crash Override.

title: Micah Elizabeth Scott
summary: Micah Elizabeth Scott, known online as scanlime, is an American engineer and artist who works on hardware reverse engineering, embedded firmware and open source hardware. She is the creator of the Fadecandy LED controller, a co-author of the Fyre rendering program, the developer of the Virtual USB Analyzer at VMware, and the author of a long-running video series documenting her reverse engineering work.

title: Orin Kerr
summary: Orin Samuel Kerr is an American legal scholar and former U.S. Department of Justice computer crime prosecutor who is widely regarded as a founding figure in the academic field of computer crime law. His work on the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) and on the Fourth Amendment's application to digital evidence has been cited by courts up to and including the U.S. Supreme Court.

title: Paras Jha
summary: Paras Jha is an American computer science student who, under the online alias "Anna-senpai," co-authored the Mirai botnet malware and pleaded guilty in federal court in December 2017 to computer crimes related to Mirai and to a separate series of denial-of-service attacks against Rutgers University.

title: Paul Le Roux
summary: Paul Le Roux is a Zimbabwe-born programmer who wrote the disk-encryption program E4M (Encryption for the Masses) in the late 1990s before building a sprawling transnational criminal organization involved in drug trafficking, arms smuggling, and murder-for-hire, which led to his 2012 arrest and 2020 sentencing.

title: Peter Tippett
summary: Peter Tippett is an American physician and software developer who founded the Cleveland software house FoundationWare, later renamed Certus International, whose commercial anti-virus products included Vaccine and NOVI. After Symantec acquired Certus International in late 1992 and folded its technology into Norton AntiVirus, Tippett moved into industry leadership, serving as president of the National Computer Security Association and later as chief scientist of ICSA.net and a senior executive at its successors TruSecure and Cybertrust.

title: Ralph Merkle
summary: Ralph C. Merkle is an American computer scientist and cryptographer who independently conceived public key cryptography as an undergraduate in 1974 and later invented Merkle trees, the hash-tree structure used in digital signatures, distributed file systems, and blockchains. He is also known for work on cryptographic hash functions, block ciphers at Xerox PARC, and, in a second career, molecular nanotechnology.

title: Randy Suess
summary: Randy Suess (1945-2019) was an American computer hobbyist who, with Ward Christensen, built CBBS, generally recognized as the first computer bulletin board system, brought online in Chicago on February 16, 1978. He later founded Chinet, one of the earliest public-access Unix systems.

title: Renee DiResta
summary: Renee DiResta is an American researcher and writer on online manipulation, propaganda, and state-sponsored influence operations, best known as lead author of a Senate Intelligence Committee report on Russia's Internet Research Agency and as technical research manager at the Stanford Internet Observatory. She is the author of Invisible Rulers (2024) and an associate research professor at Georgetown University's McCourt School of Public Policy.

title: Ross Ulbricht
summary: Ross Ulbricht is an American who created and operated the Silk Road, an early and influential dark web marketplace for illegal goods, under the alias "Dread Pirate Roberts." Convicted in 2015 and sentenced to life in prison without parole, he was granted a full and unconditional pardon by President Donald Trump in January 2025.

title: Jay Freeman
summary: Jay Freeman, known online as "saurik," is an American software developer and hacker best known for creating Cydia, the graphical package manager and alternative app distribution platform for jailbroken iOS devices.

title: Shafi Goldwasser
summary: Shafi Goldwasser is an American-Israeli computer scientist and cryptographer whose work with Silvio Micali established the theoretical foundations of modern provable security, including probabilistic encryption and zero-knowledge proofs. She and Micali received the 2012 ACM A.M. Turing Award for this body of work.

title: Silvio Micali
summary: Silvio Micali is an Italian-American computer scientist and MIT professor who co-invented probabilistic encryption and zero-knowledge proofs, work for which he shared the 2012 ACM Turing Award, and who later founded the Algorand blockchain protocol.

title: Matt Miller
summary: Matt Miller, known online as skape, is a security researcher who was a core Metasploit Framework developer from 2004 to 2008, documented the Meterpreter payload, and edited the Uninformed journal before joining Microsoft, where he worked on Windows exploit mitigation research.

title: Susan Headley
summary: Susan Headley, known by the handle Susan Thunder (also rendered Susy Thunder), is an American former phone phreak and computer intruder who was active in the Los Angeles scene of the late 1970s and early 1980s. She is remembered chiefly as an early practitioner of what she called psychological subversion, the manipulation of people rather than machines to obtain access to telephone and computer systems.

title: Taher Elgamal
